nodes.name: Read Your Site
nodes.summary: Map the sun, shelter and drainage of your plot before you buy a single plant. Most early failures are the wrong plant in the wrong place.
steps: Sketch your garden or balcony and mark north.
Check the spot at 9am, noon and 4pm and note whether it is in full sun, part shade or shade.
After heavy rain, note where water pools and where it drains away fast.
Note wind exposure and walls that hold heat.
Count hours of direct sun: full sun is 6 or more, part shade is 3 to 6, shade is under 3.
drills: Make a sun map of your whole plot on one sunny day, with three time-stamped photos.
Label each bed or pot with its sun category.
nodes.mastery: You can show a sketch of your garden with sun hours per area and name two plants suited to each zone.
mistakes: Judging the sun from a single morning visit.
Planting sun-lovers like tomatoes in 3 hours of light because the spot looks pretty.
Ignoring where water collects.

nodes.name: Tools and Safe Digging
nodes.summary: Know the handful of tools that do most of the work, and use them without wrecking your back or your plants.
steps: Get a spade, hand trowel, hand fork, hoe, secateurs and a watering can or hose with a rose.
Dig with your legs and keep the load close to your body.
Wipe and dry blades after use so they do not rust.
Sharpen secateurs and spades once a season with a file or stone.
Wear gloves and sturdy shoes, and keep tetanus vaccination up to date.
drills: Dig and refill a 30 cm square planting hole with correct posture, then dig a second one.
Clean and oil your tools at the end of a session, every session for a month.
nodes.mastery: You can name what each tool is for, and you have cleaned and sharpened your secateurs so they cut a stem cleanly in one squeeze.
mistakes: Buying cheap bendy tools that fail in the first season.
Putting tools away wet and dirty.
Digging with a rounded back and no breaks.

nodes.name: Know Your Soil
nodes.summary: Soil is sand, silt, clay and organic matter in some mix. Knowing yours tells you how it holds water and food.
steps: Dig a spade-deep hole and look at the colour, roots and worms.
Rub a moist handful between your fingers: gritty means sandy, sticky and ribbon-forming means clay, smooth and silky means silt.
Do a jar test: shake soil with water, let it settle for 24 hours and measure the layers.
Do a drainage test: fill a 30 cm hole with water, then fill it again and time how long it takes to drain.
Write down your result: sandy, loamy, silty or clay.
drills: Run the jar test on soil from two different beds and compare.
Time drainage in three spots of your garden.
nodes.mastery: You can classify your soil by feel and by jar test, and say whether it drains too fast, too slow or well.
mistakes: Testing only the top 2 cm.
Digging or working clay when it is wet, which compacts it into bricks.
Assuming bagged compost fixes a drainage problem on its own.

nodes.name: Sowing Seeds
nodes.summary: Get seeds from packet to seedling by reading the packet and giving them the depth, warmth and moisture they need.
steps: Read the packet for sowing window, depth, spacing and days to germination.
Sow at about twice the seed's width in depth, and surface-sow tiny seeds like lettuce lightly pressed in.
Water gently with a fine rose or mist so seeds do not wash away.
Label every row or pot with the name and date.
Keep the soil evenly moist, like a wrung-out sponge, until seedlings appear.
drills: Sow a row of radish or lettuce and log germination day by day.
Sow 20 seeds of one type and count how many germinate for a percentage.
nodes.mastery: You have sown a packet of seed outdoors or in trays and got at least 70 percent to true-leaf stage.
mistakes: Burying seeds too deep.
Letting the seed bed dry out for a day or two while seeds are germinating.
Sowing the whole packet in one go instead of in batches.

nodes.name: Watering Properly
nodes.summary: Water deeply and less often at the base of plants, so roots grow down and leaves stay dry.
steps: Check moisture with a finger 5 cm deep before you water.
Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves.
Water in the early morning so water is used before the heat and leaves dry quickly.
Soak slowly until moisture reaches roughly 15 to 20 cm down, rather than a daily sprinkle.
Water seedlings and new transplants more often until they are established.
drills: For a week, water only when the finger test says so, and note how often that is.
Dig down 15 cm an hour after watering to check how deep the water went.
nodes.mastery: You can show with a trowel that a watering reached 15 cm deep, and you water on a schedule set by soil checks, not the calendar.
mistakes: Light daily sprinkling that keeps roots shallow.
Watering in the evening onto leaves, which encourages mildew and slugs.
Overwatering potted plants until roots rot.

nodes.name: Weeding and Mulching
nodes.summary: Remove weeds before they seed and cover bare soil with mulch to hold moisture and block new weeds.
steps: Pull annual weeds when small, after rain, and get the root.
Remove perennial weeds like dandelion and bindweed by digging out the whole root.
Never let weeds flower and set seed.
Spread 5 to 7 cm of mulch such as compost, leaf mould or wood chips over damp soil, keeping it a few cm off stems.
Top up mulch each spring.
drills: Clear and mulch a 2 square metre bed and compare weed counts after 3 weeks to an unmulched bed.
Spend 10 minutes weeding twice a week for a month.
nodes.mastery: You have a mulched bed that is visibly weed-free after four weeks, and can name three weeds and how each spreads.
mistakes: Mulching over dry soil, which locks the dryness in.
Piling mulch against stems, which causes rot.
Hoeing perennial weeds into pieces that regrow.

nodes.name: Planting Out Seedlings
nodes.summary: Move young plants into the ground or pots with minimum shock so they establish quickly.
steps: Harden off seedlings by putting them outside for a few hours a day for 7 to 10 days.
Dig a hole about twice the width of the root ball.
Water the plant in its pot first, tease out circling roots and set it at the same depth it grew at.
Backfill, firm gently and water thoroughly.
Shade and water new plants daily for the first week in hot weather.
drills: Plant out six seedlings and track how many survive a month.
Practise teasing roots on a pot-bound plant from a garden centre.
nodes.mastery: You have planted out at least a dozen seedlings or plants with 90 percent surviving to four weeks.
mistakes: Skipping hardening off and shocking plants with sun and wind.
Planting too deep, especially woody plants.
Not watering in after planting.

nodes.name: pH and Plant Food
nodes.summary: Test pH and learn what nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium do, so you feed plants for a reason.
steps: Buy a basic soil pH kit or send a sample to a local soil lab.
Know the targets: most vegetables like pH 6.0 to 7.0, blueberries and rhododendrons like acidic soil near 4.5 to 5.5.
Learn the N-P-K roles: nitrogen for leaves, phosphorus for roots and flowers, potassium for fruit and general health.
Raise pH with garden lime; lower it slowly with sulphur or by growing acid-lovers in pots.
Feed according to the crop: leafy plants want nitrogen, tomatoes want potash once fruiting.
drills: Test pH in three beds and record the results.
Read the N-P-K numbers on three fertilisers and say which crops suit each.
nodes.mastery: You have a pH reading for each bed, can say which crops suit it, and can justify one amendment or feed you applied.
mistakes: Adding lime or fertiliser without testing.
Over-feeding nitrogen, which gives leaf and no fruit.
Treating yellow leaves as hunger when the cause is overwatering.

nodes.name: Composting
nodes.summary: Turn kitchen scraps and garden waste into crumbly compost, the single best thing you can add to soil.
steps: Pick a bin or open heap at least 1 metre cube if you want it to heat up.
Mix greens (kitchen scraps, grass) and browns (cardboard, dry leaves) at roughly 1 part green to 2 parts brown by volume.
Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge and turn every few weeks.
Avoid meat, dairy, cooked food and diseased plants in a basic heap.
Use it when dark, crumbly and earthy-smelling, usually in 3 to 12 months.
drills: Build a first heap and keep a log of temperature and moisture weekly.
Fix a smelly or dry heap by adjusting browns, greens and water.
nodes.mastery: You have produced a batch of finished, dark and crumbly compost and spread it on a bed.
mistakes: Adding only grass clippings, which turns slimy and smelly.
Letting the heap get dry or waterlogged.
Adding weeds in seed and perennial roots to a cold heap.

nodes.name: Starting Seeds Indoors
nodes.summary: Raise tomatoes, peppers and brassicas under light and warmth weeks before the weather allows.
steps: Use fresh seed-starting mix, which is fine and low in nutrients.
Sow in trays or modules 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost for tomatoes and peppers.
Give 14 to 16 hours a day of strong light close to the seedlings, with a grow light if the windowsill is weak.
Prick out or pot on when the first true leaves appear.
Water from below and keep air moving to prevent damping off.
drills: Raise 12 tomato seedlings and note their height weekly.
Compare seedlings on a windowsill to ones under a light.
nodes.mastery: You have raised a tray of stocky, green seedlings, not leggy or damped off, to planting-out size.
mistakes: Starting too early so plants outgrow their pots.
Weak light that makes tall, pale seedlings.
Reusing old soil that carries damping-off disease.

nodes.name: Basic Pruning
nodes.summary: Cut for health, shape and flowering using clean cuts at the right time of year.
steps: Use sharp, clean secateurs and cut just above an outward-facing bud at a slight angle.
Always start by removing the three Ds: dead, diseased, damaged.
Then remove crossing or rubbing branches.
Prune spring-flowering shrubs just after flowering and summer-flowering ones in late winter.
Do not remove more than about a third of a plant at once.
drills: Prune one shrub, with before and after photos.
Identify five shrubs in your area and write when each should be pruned.
nodes.mastery: You can prune a shrub correctly for its type, with clean cuts above buds and a better shape afterwards.
mistakes: Pruning spring bloomers in winter and removing the flowers.
Cutting flush to the trunk or leaving stubs.
Taking off too much in one go.

nodes.name: Identifying Pests and Disease
nodes.summary: Know the common pests, diseases and deficiencies by sight, so you treat the right problem.
steps: Inspect plants weekly, including the undersides of leaves.
Learn the usual suspects: aphids, slugs and snails, cabbage white caterpillars, spider mites, powdery mildew, blight.
Check whether damage is a bug (holes, chewing, trails), a disease (spots, powder, wilt) or a care issue (yellowing, scorching).
Photograph and compare with a trusted extension service guide.
Learn which insects are friends: ladybirds, hoverflies, lacewings and ground beetles.
drills: Do a 10-minute weekly pest patrol for a month and keep a log.
Identify five problems in photos from an extension service site without checking the answer.
nodes.mastery: You can correctly name the cause of five different plant problems in your own or a friend's garden.
mistakes: Spraying before identifying, which also kills beneficial insects.
Mistaking overwatering or nutrient shortage for a disease.
Leaving infected leaves on the ground.

nodes.name: Building and Filling Beds
nodes.summary: Build a bed or container set-up with the right size, depth and soil mix for the plants you want.
steps: Keep beds no wider than 1.2 metres so you can reach the middle without stepping on the soil.
Make them 20 to 30 cm deep for most veg, deeper for carrots and parsnips.
Fill with a blend such as roughly 60 percent topsoil, 30 percent compost and 10 percent coarse sand or grit; avoid pure bagged compost.
Put beds in full sun and where water does not pool.
Add a layer of cardboard underneath to suppress weeds.
drills: Plan a 1.2 by 2.4 m bed on paper with plant spacing.
Build one and plant the first crop.
nodes.mastery: You have built and planted a bed that is workable from the edges, drains properly and has grown a crop.
mistakes: Making beds too wide to reach.
Filling with cheap light compost that sinks and dries out.
Putting them in shade for convenience.

nodes.name: Crop Rotation and Companions
nodes.summary: Moving plant families around beds each year breaks pest and disease cycles and balances soil nutrients.
steps: Group your crops by family: brassicas, legumes, roots, alliums, and nightshades and cucurbits.
Divide the veg plot into four beds and move each group one bed on every year.
Follow heavy-feeding brassicas with legumes, which add nitrogen.
Keep potatoes and tomatoes away from where their family grew last year.
Use companions such as marigolds, nasturtiums or alliums where evidence supports them, but do not rely on them.
drills: Write a four-year rotation plan for your plot.
Mark last year's crop positions on a map before you plant.
nodes.mastery: You have a written four-bed rotation, with each crop family placed correctly for this and next year.
mistakes: Planting tomatoes in the same spot each year.
Forgetting that cabbages, kale and radishes are all in one family.
Trusting folk companion planting claims without checking them.

nodes.name: Succession Sowing
nodes.summary: Sow little and often so crops arrive across months, not in one glut.
steps: List fast crops that suit repeat sowing: lettuce, radish, spinach, beetroot, carrots, bush beans.
Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks.
Fill gaps left by early harvests with a new crop straight away.
Choose varieties for the season: bolt-resistant lettuce in summer, hardy kinds for autumn.
Keep a sowing calendar showing dates and harvests.
drills: Sow lettuce every two weeks for 10 weeks and log harvests.
Plan a bed that holds three different crops in one season.
nodes.mastery: You have had a continuous supply of at least two crops over 8 weeks or more, with a log of sowing dates.
mistakes: Sowing everything at once and ending up with more than you can eat.
Using lettuce varieties that bolt in midsummer heat.
Leaving beds bare after a harvest.

nodes.name: Integrated Pest Management
nodes.summary: Control pests with a ladder of steps, starting with prevention and using chemicals only as a last resort.
steps: Prevent: choose resistant varieties, rotate crops, keep plants healthy and space them for airflow.
Block: use fine insect mesh, collars and barriers.
Remove by hand: squash eggs, pick off caterpillars and slugs at dusk, wash aphids off with water.
Attract predators with flowers, a pond and undisturbed corners.
If you must spray, use the most selective product, follow the label and spray in the evening away from pollinators.
drills: Protect a brassica bed with mesh from planting day and compare it with an unprotected row.
Count aphids and ladybirds weekly for a month.
nodes.mastery: You can show a growing season where a main pest was managed with prevention and barriers, with crop damage under 10 percent.
mistakes: Reaching straight for a broad-spectrum spray.
Mesh with gaps at the edges.
Spraying open flowers where bees feed.

nodes.name: Efficient Irrigation
nodes.summary: Drip lines, soaker hoses and rain capture water plants exactly where needed and save time.
steps: Install a water butt or other rain capture on a downpipe.
Lay drip line or soaker hose along each bed, with a pressure reducer if needed.
Put it on a timer so watering happens before dawn.
Mulch over the line to cut evaporation.
Check for blocked emitters and leaks monthly.
drills: Set up drip irrigation on one bed and measure water use for a week.
Check soil moisture across the bed at 5 points after a cycle.
nodes.mastery: You have a working drip or soaker system on a timer which waters a bed evenly, confirmed by soil checks.
mistakes: Running the system for too short a time to wet the root zone.
Never checking emitters for clogs.
Watering to a schedule regardless of rain.

nodes.name: Season and Frost Planning
nodes.summary: Plan every sowing and planting around your local frost dates, soil temperature and day length.
steps: Find your average last spring and first autumn frost dates from a local weather or extension source.
Work back from the last frost using seed packet weeks to get indoor sowing dates.
Sort crops into hardy, half-hardy and tender and plant each accordingly.
Use cloches, row cover or cold frames to extend the season by 2 to 4 weeks.
Write a month-by-month task calendar for your plot.
drills: Make a one-page calendar for ten crops with sow, plant and harvest dates.
Keep a weather and frost log for a season.
nodes.mastery: You have a written year plan with local frost dates, and no crop was lost to a frost you could have predicted.
mistakes: Planting tender crops on the first warm weekend.
Using packet dates written for another climate.
Not checking the forecast for late frost warnings.

nodes.name: Fruit Trees and Bushes
nodes.summary: Plant, train and prune apples, pears, berries and currants so they crop reliably year after year.
steps: Choose rootstock for your space and check pollination partners and chill hours.
Plant bare-root trees in winter, with the graft union above soil.
Train a basic open-centre or central-leader shape in the first three years.
Prune apples and pears in winter and stone fruit in summer to avoid disease.
Thin fruit in June so the remainder grow larger and trees crop every year.
drills: Prune a mature apple tree with an experienced gardener beside you.
Thin fruitlets to one per cluster, 10 to 15 cm apart.
nodes.mastery: You have trained or restored a fruit tree to good shape and picked a decent crop from it.
mistakes: Planting a variety with no pollination partner.
Pruning stone fruit in winter, when silver leaf and canker spread.
Burying the graft union.

nodes.name: Seed Saving
nodes.summary: Save seed from your best plants so you have free, locally adapted crops from year to year.
steps: Start with self-pollinating crops: beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes.
Use open-pollinated varieties, not F1 hybrids, which will not come true.
Pick the best plants and leave fruit or pods until fully ripe.
Dry thoroughly and store labelled in paper envelopes in a cool, dry, dark place.
Test germination on damp paper before sowing.
drills: Save and germination-test seed from three crops.
Isolate and save seed from one cross-pollinating crop.
nodes.mastery: You have grown a crop from seed you saved yourself, with germination rate of 80 percent or better.
mistakes: Saving from F1 hybrids.
Storing seed damp or warm.
Letting varieties of the same species cross-pollinate.

nodes.name: Building Living Soil
nodes.summary: Feed the soil life of fungi, bacteria and worms rather than just the plants, and cut digging to protect the soil structure.
steps: Switch to no-dig on at least one bed: lay 10 cm of compost on top each year.
Grow cover crops like crimson clover, winter rye or phacelia over bare soil.
Use a worm bin or hot compost to make top-quality compost.
Avoid synthetic fertiliser overuse and avoid leaving bare soil.
Measure progress with organic matter, earthworm counts and soil structure.
drills: Count earthworms in a 30 cm cube of soil before and after a year of no-dig.
Compare yield in a no-dig and a dug bed.
nodes.mastery: You have a bed run for a full year with no digging and cover crops, with measurable improvement in soil structure and a good crop.
mistakes: Switching to no-dig on compacted soil without loosening it once.
Using unfinished compost, which robs nitrogen.
Leaving soil bare in winter.

nodes.name: Cover Crops and Green Manures
nodes.summary: Grow plants for the soil, not the table, to fix nitrogen, suppress weeds and add organic matter.
steps: Pick by season: winter rye or field beans in autumn, buckwheat or phacelia in summer gaps, clover for long cover.
Sow after harvest, broadcast and rake in.
Cut before flowering and either leave as mulch or dig lightly in.
Wait 2 to 4 weeks before sowing small seeds after incorporating.
Fit green manures into your rotation plan.
drills: Sow a cover crop on one bed after summer harvest and plant into it next spring.
Compare nitrogen-hungry crop yield on cover-cropped and bare beds.
nodes.mastery: You have used a cover crop on a bed over winter and planted a following crop that did well on it.
mistakes: Letting it flower and set seed in the bed.
Sowing too late for it to establish.
Planting straight after incorporation.

nodes.name: Year-Round Productive Garden
nodes.summary: Run a garden that produces something worth harvesting in every month of the year, using planning, protection and good timing.
steps: Plan crops for each season including hardy winter veg, perennials and stored crops.
Use cold frames, polytunnels or row covers for winter harvests.
Run multiple beds on a rotation with succession and cover crops.
Keep records of sowing, harvest weights and pests.
Review every autumn and adjust the plan.
drills: Harvest and photograph something from your garden on the first of every month for 12 months.
Weigh the harvest and tot up total yield per square metre.
nodes.mastery: You have a dated photo and harvest log showing fresh produce from your own garden in all 12 months of a year.
mistakes: Planning only for summer.
No records, so you repeat mistakes.
Overextending the plot beyond the time you have.

nodes.name: Self-Sustaining Garden Ecosystem
nodes.summary: A mature garden that feeds its own soil, saves its own seed, supports wildlife and needs few outside inputs.
steps: Close the loop: make all compost on site and use no peat or bought fertiliser.
Save seed from at least a dozen crops.
Establish perennial crops: fruit, rhubarb, asparagus and herbs.
Create habitat: pond, hedge, flower margins and log piles.
Mentor a beginner and teach them something from every tier.
drills: Audit one year's inputs and outputs of your garden in a spreadsheet.
Run a workshop or garden walk for others.
nodes.mastery: Across a full year you used only home-made compost and saved seed for at least ten crops, with perennials and wildlife habitat in place, and can show the records.
mistakes: Chasing self-sufficiency while ignoring yield and enjoyment.
Letting the garden become too big to maintain.
Neglecting records.
